body:
Systolic array (matmul accelerator)

The matmul accelerator is a 16×16 systolic array. It tiles each matmul internally onto the 16×16 array, and it also enables tiling at the software level, so matrices larger than the array are split into tiles in software and run as a sequence of matmuls.

Measured throughput on the DE1-SoC (N×N int8 matmul), systolic array vs CPU baseline (2 threads, NEON SIMD kernel, 32×32 tiling):
- 64×64: 6.043 vs 4.989 GOP/s (1.21×)
- 128×128: 11.392 vs 6.083 GOP/s (1.87×)
- 256×256: 18.302 vs 6.654 GOP/s (2.75×)
- 512×512: 18.884 vs 6.950 GOP/s (2.72×)

Full table: ECE496 Files & Data → Matmul throughput: CPU baseline vs systolic array.

MNN backend / TinyViT integration (Nov 3, 2026)

The full TinyViT model runs on the DE1-SoC with one attention matrix multiplication offloaded to the FPGA; the remaining operations run on the CPU. Both synthetic test inputs and six physical matrix tests passed.

In single-run tests, offload made full-model inference 5.74% faster on zero input and 2.71% slower on nonuniform input. A reliable speedup and accuracy on real images are not yet established.

Next: repeat matched benchmarks, measure offload overhead, and test accuracy on real images.

WIKI Update

- Added editable member updates, biweekly team summaries, and meeting notes.
- Organized project results, Gantt chart, and ECE496 files into dedicated tabs.
- Added in-page forms to create, edit, and remove entries.

SIMD Measurement

- Tested 32×32 int8 matrix multiplication on the board’s Cortex-A9 CPU.
- Compiled with GCC, using -O3 -mcpu=cortex-a9 -mfpu=neon.
- Compared plain C code with NEON SIMD, using the same calculations and quantization.
- Used 1,000 warmup runs and 10,000 timed runs, then compared median times.
- Plain C took 202.12 µs; SIMD took 94.67 µs, making SIMD 2.13× faster.
- SIMD results matched the plain C reference.

Softmax Implementation

- Built 16-bit fixed-point softmax, supporting up to 196 values per row.
- Used a lookup table to calculate exponential values, with 3,073 useful entries stored in 4,096 × 16 bits (8 KiB).
- Changed division to use restoring unsigned division, which calculates one bit per clock cycle and finishes in 33 clock cycles, reducing hardware usage and improving timing.
- Tested 147 rows and 8,666 outputs; all results exactly matched the Python integer reference.
- The standalone module passed 90 MHz timing and used 222 ALMs and 10 M10K memory blocks.
- Next step: connect softmax to the matmul accelerator and test the complete system.

GELU Integration and Timing

- Confirmed bias + GELU is connected to accel_top and processes results when the CPU reads the output buffer.
- Supports 16 int8 values at once, with a 256-byte bias buffer that the CPU can load.
- The standalone module now passes 90 MHz timing; logic usage dropped from 1,707 to 957 ALMs.

Baseline and profiling (Nov 3, 2026)

- Full TinyViT-21M inference latency: 7.64 s (FP32, 1 thread), 5.07 s (INT8, 1 thread), and 3.19 s (INT8, 2 threads).
- Profiled FP32 and INT8 operators. GELU and GEMM were the largest INT8 groups, taking about 30.7% and 27.0% of logged layer time, respectively.
- Compared FP32 and INT8 on 2,000 ImageNet images; INT8 had a reported 1.3% drop in top-1 accuracy.
- Next: repeat matched CPU/FPGA benchmarks, measure transfer and control overhead, and compare integrated accuracy and latency with the CPU baseline.

Peripheral setup (Nov 3, 2026)

- Connected a USB camera to the DE1-SoC and confirmed the board receives live image input.
- Next: connect camera capture and preprocessing to the FPGA-accelerated model, verify live predictions, and measure camera-to-classification latency.

title: This week
body:
Yixin (Stephanie) — TinyViT CPU–FPGA integration (Nov 17, 2026)

- Integrated 30 static-weight INT8 matmuls into the MNN-controlled TinyViT graph on the HPS CPU. Selected QKV/output projections and MLP layers run on FPGA; dynamic attention matmuls, softmax, normalization, residuals and the remaining model run on CPU. Execution is synchronous, with no CPU/FPGA overlap.
- Added four resident FC1→activation→FC2 pairs. Hidden activations stay in FPGA RAM in row blocks, skipping 16 CPU operations and reducing host payload by about 616 KB per image. Weights remain cached in HPS DDR and are transferred in tiles.
- Mixed precision retained 148/200 correct classifications versus FP32’s 149/200 on a separate CPU holdout; broad quantization achieved only 21/200. Integrated FPGA accuracy is not established by this CPU test.
- Mean model inference: FP32 CPU 1,155.982 ms → mixed-precision CPU 1,080.605 ms → separate FPGA offloads 1,048.245 ms → resident fusion 1,006.955 ms (20 random RGB images, 2 CPU threads, 90 MHz FPGA, detailed profiling disabled).
- Final latency improves 12.89% versus FP32 CPU and 6.82% versus mixed-precision CPU; resident fusion contributes 41.289 ms of the saving.

Softmax Implementation

- Changed the external interface to signed INT8 scores and probability codes 0–127, supporting 1–196 values per row. Uses a 256 × 16-bit exponential LUT and 23-cycle unsigned restoring division.
- Passed 9 software tests and bit-exact RTL checks on 578 rows / 25,999 outputs. Standalone routed timing passed 90 MHz using 175 ALMs, 3 M10Ks and 0 DSPs (setup slack +3.894 ns).
- On 10 images, probability relative RMSE was 6.634% and attention-context (P@V) relative RMSE was 2.532%. Independent INT8 rounding does not enforce row sums of 1; 196-key model accuracy still needs validation.
- Next: resolve scale/layout interfaces and integrate with matmul and the full SoC. Board operation and end-to-end speedup have not been tested.

LayerNorm Implementation and Timing

- Built signed INT8 input/output LayerNorm for 1–576 channels, with INT8 gamma/beta supplied per row. Uses a 25-cycle digit-by-digit integer square root and 41-cycle restoring division; internal normalization retains 14 fractional bits.
- Calibrated scales on 7 images and checked 3 held-out images: validation relative RMSE was 3.485%, with 0.0961% input clipping. Top-1 predictions matched on 10 isolated replacement tests; this is not a dataset accuracy result.
- Passed 9 software tests and bit-exact RTL checks on 744 rows / 200,296 outputs. Pipelining and proven width reductions preserved integer results and closed standalone 90 MHz timing: 510 ALMs, 4 M10Ks and 8 DSPs (setup slack +0.321 ns).
- Next: validate more model sites, channel ordering and parameter/scaling interfaces, then integrate, recheck full-SoC timing and test on the board.

Tiffany (Yiling) — USB camera and HPS-only live classification (Nov 17, 2026)

- Completed USB camera peripheral setup on the DE1-SoC and verified live image capture through Linux/UVC.
- Created a live image-classification demo with TinyViT inference running on the HPS CPU, displaying the camera feed and predicted ImageNet class labels on the connected computer.
- Added a recording of the earlier CPU-only inference demo to ECE496 Files & Data. That recording uses Windows preprocessing; it does not document the subsequent HPS-local preprocessing work.

Next steps
- Integrate all team members’ software and FPGA hardware code to run end-to-end live image classification on the hybrid CPU–FPGA design, keeping image capture and preprocessing on HPS.
- Build and validate a timing measurement tool to separate capture/decode, preprocessing, CPU inference, FPGA computation, HPS–FPGA transfer/control, and result-display overhead. Record per-frame measurements and end-to-end latency to identify bottlenecks and compare the HPS-only and hybrid pipelines under matched settings.
